stem: Which of the following statements is correct regarding this patient's condition?
options: It is associated with a reduced diffusion capacity for carbon monoxide
Rheumatoid factor is positive in more than 90% of cases
It is associated with an erosive arthritis
It occurs more commonly in men
Raynaud's phenomenon is a feature in ~10%
explanation:
The slide shows a patient with systemic sclerosis (SSc).
Features present include:MicrostomiaFacial telangiectasia, andBeaking of the nose.

stem:
A 78-year-old gentleman with learning diﬃculties, is admitted to hospital with an acute exacerbation of congestive cardiac failure.
He is currently on bumetanide 2 mg TDS, carvedilol 25 mg OD, perindopril 4 mg BD and was recently started on spironolactone 100 mg OD.
On examination you notice severe raised plaques of psoriasis covering his chest, elbows, knees and scalp. He mentions that he has beentreating it with topical creams for years but has seen no improvement and did not seek medical advice because he was too embarrassed.
What treatment would you recommend for his psoriasis?
options: Start on oral steroids and taper off gradually
explanation:
The safest treatment - that which produces the best clinical effect with minimal side effects in this patient - would be psoralen andultraviolet light (PUVA). It requires his carer bringing him in for appointments and the clinic staff recording his progress.
Emollients, baths and use of methotrexate require a fair amount of input from the patient in order to be effective and safe, whichmay not be the best option in this man.
Oral steroids are contraindicated in psoriasis and although one may see an initial improvement, a very serious rebound effect may beseen.
Certain drugs can exacerbate psoriasis (such as beta blockers) so the list of medications ought to be reviewed.

stem:
A 26-year-old male epileptic is admitted with temperature and rash.
Over the last one week a rash has developed and he has become increasingly ill. Recently he has had some problems with epileptic controland has commenced carbamazepine with valproate.
Examination reveals an unwell patient with a temperature of 39°C, a diffuse erythematous, painful rash with evidence of some lateral slidingof these erythematous areas on palpation.
There is also blistering and inﬂammation of the oral cavity.
What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
This patient's presentation and clinical description suggests a diagnosis of toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) due to carbamazepinetherapy.
TEN is a severe mucocutaneous exfoliative disease with an uncertain pathogenesis and a high mortality rate.
It is diﬃcult to say whether it is another variant of Stevens-Johnson syndrome and treatment of both are similar.
It is often idiopathic but may be associated with:Viral infectionsLeukaemiaLymphoma, andDrugs (in particular sulphonamides and anticonvulsants).
The suggested association with carbamazipine in this case makes toxic shock syndrome due to Staph. aureus remote, which likepustular psoriasis would not be expected to affect the mucous membranes.

stem:
A 45-year-old gardener was referred to the dermatology clinic with a well-circumscribed, raised erythematous lesion on his ﬁnger.
The lesion had enlarged steadily over the previous three weeks, was tender and bled easily when touched.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Pyogenic granuloma (lobular capillary haemangioma) is a benign vascular lesion of the skin and mucosa. The cause is unknown.
The name is a double misnomer - the lesion is neither pyogenic nor a granuloma.
Pyogenic granulomata are usually solitary lesions, appearing as a glistening red papule or nodule that is prone to bleeding andulceration. Lesions often grow rapidly (over weeks), frequently occurring at sites of trauma and commonly involve the digits, arms,head and face. Pathologically, it is an inﬂammatory lesion composed of granulation tissue and chronic inﬂammatory cells.
Keratoacanthoma is a low-grade malignancy that originates in the pilosebaceous glands. Clinically and pathologically the lesionsresemble squamous cell carcinoma. Lesions typically are solitary with a central area of ulceration that may contain a characteristickeratin plug.
Cutaneous anthrax would not be expected on the basis of the history given. Anthrax lesions begin as reddened, indurated papules,later becoming necrotic with a characteristic black centre (eschar).
Pictures of cutaneous anthrax appear in the MRCP Part 2 examination, though the usual history given is of someone from (or whohas visited) the Middle East and had contact with cattle/sheep/goats.
Malignant melanomas may occur at any site, but given the context provided in this case, are a less likely option.
Mycobacterium marinum is the cause of ﬁsh tank granuloma. Lesions are ovoid and usually occur on the hands (following contactwith ﬁsh). Fishermen, ﬁshmongers and tropical ﬁsh enthusiasts are susceptible.

stem: Which of the following is the most important in establishing the cause of these lesions?
explanation:
Erythema nodosum is shown in the slide.
Erythema nodosum is commonly idiopathic, although streptococcal infection is the most common underlying cause.
However, the commonest potentially serious causes (and therefore those that should be excluded ﬁrst) include sarcoidosis andtuberculosis. A chest x ray is an important investigation to exclude both of these causes.
Erythema nodosum can also be related to drugs such as the oral contraceptive pill, sulphonamides and penicillins. Rarer causesinclude inﬂammatory bowel disease, tuberculosis, Behçet's disease and other connective tissue disorders.

stem: Which of the following is not a recognised complication of this condition?
explanation:
The slide shows the typical 'plucked chicken skin' appearance of pseudoxanthoma elasticum.
The disease is rare and is characterised by progressive calciﬁcation and degeneration of elastic ﬁbres and primarily affects the skin,retina and cardiovascular system. Cutaneous manifestations are typical. Small, yellow papules of 1-5 mm in diameter are seen andmay coalesce to form plaques.

stem:
This patient has an abnormal chest x ray.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The slide shows cutaneous tuberculosis (lupus vulgaris).
Cutaneous TB usually occurs due to spread from an endogenous source; more than 80% of cases occur on the face and neck.

stem:
A 42-year-old man presented to the dermatology outpatient clinic with a pruritic photosensitive skin rash.
His liver function tests were abnormal.
Histology from his liver biopsy is shown.
What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT) is associated with reduced hepatic uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase activity and risk factors such asalcohol abuse, medication (for example, oral contraceptives and certain other drugs) and hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection.
When exposed to light, uroporphyrinogen generates free radicals that cause blistering of the skin.
PCT can be treated with phlebotomy to deplete the excess iron stores that exacerbate the porphyria.

stem:
A 45-year-old dockyard worker presented with symptoms of fatigue and general malaise, especially after working outside. He also reporteddeveloping ulcers on his hands after minor trauma.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT) is associated with deﬁciency of hepatic uroporphyrinogen (URO) decarboxylase.
The major clinical feature is cutaneous photosensitivity. Bullae develop on sun-exposed areas and lesions heal slowly, leaving scars.
Porphyrins are increased in liver, plasma, urine and stool. Porphobilinigen (PBG) is normal.

stem: With which of the following is this condition associated?
explanation:
Yellow nail syndrome is caused by hypoplastic lymphatics and is characterised by the triad of:LymphoedemaPleural effusions, andYellow discolouration of the nails.
Approximately 40% of patients also have bronchiectasis.

stem:
This patient originally presented ten years ago with a pruritic rash on her abdomen. These lesions now cover her entire body.
This disease is caused by inﬁltration of which of the following?
explanation:
The diagnosis is mycosis fungoides, a cutaneous T cell lymphoma.
The disease presents as a pruritic eczematous rash (the pre-malignant stage) and develops telangiectasias and areas of 'cigarettepaper' atrophy.
As malignancy develops, nodular lesions appear and proceed to become necrotic.
Further Reading:1. Elmer KB, George RM. Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma presenting as benign dermatoses. Am Fam Physician. 1999;59:2809-13.

stem:
On skin examination of a patient, you notice a scaly, erythematous thickened plaque with accentuation of normal skin markings.
How is this surface change best described?
explanation:
Licheniﬁcation of the skin is due to epidermal thickening characterised by visible and palpable thickening of the skin withaccentuation of skin markings.
Atrophy of the skin may be due to loss of epidermis, dermis or subcutaneous tissue. Thinning of the epidermis presents as skin thatappears thin and translucent. Thinning of the dermis and subcutaneous tissue leads to a depression in the skin.
Fissures are cracks in the skin that are narrow but deep.
Telangiectasias are collections of enlarged capillaries visible on the skin or mucous membranes.
Ulcers are seen as discontinuity of the skin with complete loss of the epidermis and often portions of the dermis and subcutaneousfat.

stem:
This 19-year-old woman presented to the Emergency department complaining of painful legs.
What is the most likely cause for these lesions?
explanation:
Erythema nodosum is characterised by the presence of tender subcutaneous nodules, usually on the shins.
Histology of these lesions shows a vasculitis of small venules and panniculitis. The commonest cause is streptococcal infection.
Other common common causes include:Other upper respiratory tract infectionsSarcoidosis, andInﬂammatory bowel disease.
Less common causes are:TBHistoplasmosisCoccidioidomycosisPsittacosis

stem:
This gentleman's condition worsens in the summer and following ingestion of alcohol
Which of the following therapies is the most appropriate for inducing its remission?
explanation:
Porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT) is associated with deﬁciency of hepatic uroporphyrinogen (URO) decarboxylase. Cutaneousphotosensitivity is the predominant clinical ﬁnding.
Excess alcohol, iron and oestrogen are common precipitants. The condition may be familial.
Treatment is with withdrawal of the precipitant. Venesection is effective (450 ml/week) until haemoglobin is 120 g/L.

stem:
Botulinum toxin type A has many applications in everyday medical practise.
Which of the following is a recognised indication for the toxin?
options: Muscle rigidity, for example, Parkinson's disease
Muscle spasticity, for example, cerebral palsy
Muscle ﬂaccidity, for example, polio affecting lower motor neurones
Muscle atrophy, for example, motor neurone disease
explanation:
Botulinum toxin type A (or trade name Botox®) acts by decreasing transmission of acetylcholine across the neuromuscular junctionin striated muscles, so inducing a temporary ﬂaccid paralysis in the muscle into which it is injected.
Wrist and hand disability due to upper limb spasticity associated with stroke in adults, and use in cases of muscle spasticity, such ascases of cerebral palsy are well recognised indications for the use of Botox®.
Though not licensed, Botox has been used in other medical conditions, including:Primary axillary hyperhidrosisBlepharospasmStrabismus, andCervical dystonia.
Reference:
Electronic Medicines Compendium (eMC). Botox 100 Units.

stem:
On skin examination of a patient presenting with a rash, you notice an erythematous, scaly, raised lesion measuring 6 cm in diameter.
How would this lesion best be described?
explanation:
A plaque is a descriptive term for a skin lesion that is raised and greater than 1 cm in diameter.
An area of altered skin colour is a macule irrespective of the size.
A papule is a raised lesion less than 1 cm in diameter.
An ulcer is a discontinuity of the skin with complete loss of the epidermis and often portions of the dermis and subcutaneous fat.
A vesicle is a ﬂuid-ﬁlled, well-circumscribed raised lesion.

stem:
This infant presents with this rash a few days after birth. It worsens on sun exposure.
Which of the following is a recognised long-term complication?
explanation:
This infant has neonatal lupus. He presents with a characteristic peri-orbital 'raccoon-eyes' rash.
Other similar pink to red macules, which may have an annular conﬁguration, may be seen on the scalp, face and extremities. Themother is usually positive for anti-Ro or anti-La antibodies but may not have overt lupus erythematosus.
Congenital heart block is sequela that may occur in some infants with neonatal lupus, sometimes requiring pace-maker insertion.
The other manifestations listed here may also be seen in neonatal lupus but they resolve after a few months and do not lead topermanent sequelae.

stem:
A 40-year-old male presents with this lesion on his leg which has been present for approximately three months and is minimally painful.
He has also been aware of recurrent bouts of abdominal pain and bloody diarrhoea.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
This picture shows pyoderma gangrenosum.
Estimates of the prevalence in inﬂammatory bowel disease (IBD) range between 2% and 5%. It tends to be associated with colonicinvolvement and is perhaps slightly more common in patients with UC. The clinical presentation here favours a diagnosis of UC overCrohn's.
It is most common on the lower limb and in scars or sites of previous trauma. It is treated by immunosupression. Lesions begin assmall papules or pustules before breaking down into an ulcer. Ulcers are deep with a violaeceous border and edge which overhangsthe ulcer base.

stem:
This 52-year-old Greek woman presented with a right popliteal deep vein thrombosis.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Behcet's disease is a rare multisystem vasculitis more common in males than females.
Clinical features include the classical triad of:1. Recurrent oral ulceration2. Recurrent genital ulceration, and3. Iritis.
Other features include:FeverAbdominal painDiarrhoea

stem:
An 18-year-old woman presented with a pruritic rash which had started as a single lesion on her abdomen two weeks previously with multiplesmaller lesions developing over the chest and abdomen.
She was known to have asthma and hay fever, and was taking salbutamol inhalers. There was a family history of diabetes. A urine examinationwas negative for glucose.
Examination revealed a scaly rash over the abdomen and chest wall (see slide).
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
This is the classical history of pityriasis rosea.
There is a history of a herald patch, which presents as a single large erythematous plaque on the trunk. This is followed by multipleerythematous plaques along the rib lines on the chest and abdomen, within a few weeks of the herald patch.
The condition is self limiting, can be pruritic or asymptomatic and usually lasts six to eight weeks. The aetiology is unknown. Noparticular treatment is necessary, although moisturisers can help the pruritus.

stem:
This patient was admitted to hospital with severe central abdominal pain.
What name is given to this appearance?
explanation:
Typical lesions of eruptive xanthomata are shown: raised lesions, typically occurring on extensor surfaces.
Eruptive xanthomata occur in hyperlipidaemic states associated with hypertriglyceridaemia.
Well-recognised associations of hypertriglyceridaemia include acute pancreatitis and lipaemia retinalis.

stem:
A healthy 12-year-old boy presents with a three week history of localised hair loss over the vertex of his scalp. There is no associated itch orpain over the patch.
On examination, you notice a localised, non-scarring patch of alopecia. On gentle traction, several hairs, easily dislodged from the peripheryof the lesion, are noted to be tapered toward the base.
What is this condition?
explanation:
Alopecia areata is common in children as well as adults. It presents with localised patches of non-scarring hair loss. Remaining hairshave a characteristic 'exclamation mark' appearance, and are tapered towards the base. More severe involvement may present asalopecia totalis (total loss of scalp hair) or alopecia universalis (total loss of all body hair).
Androgenetic alopecia presents after puberty as a more diffuse slow hair loss with characteristic loss over the temporal regions andvertex in males.
Discoid lupus erythematosus (DLE) presents as scarring alopecia. Areas of alopecia are usually atrophic with visible loss of hairfollicles. Patients may have DLE lesions elsewhere. If not treated early, hair loss is usually irreversible.

stem:
A young woman presents to clinic with a three week history of intermittent joint pain and raised rash over lower legs (picture). Shecomplained of pain on palpation of the rash on the lower legs.
There was no history of recent travel and no other recent illnesses. She had a previous history of type 1 diabetes, for which she receives basalbolus insulin therapy. She had a family history of diabetes on her maternal side and psoriasis on her paternal side.
What investigation should be performed next?
explanation:
The picture shows erythema nodosum.
This is inﬂammation of the subcutaneous tissue (panniculitis) and is tender and palpable. It has a number of causes.

stem:
This 34-year-old female presents with a one month history of weight loss, fatigue and this painless rash on her shin.
Which of the following investigations would you choose for this patient?
explanation: This is pre-tibial myxoedema with slightly raised, pinkish, indurated patches usually on the fronts of the shins or dorsum of the footand often associated with acropachy.

stem:
This 52-year-old female presents with a one day history of fever and this facial appearance.
The patient is penicillin allergic having had a problems with facial swelling previously.
Which of the following antibiotics would be the most appropriate treatment for this patient?
explanation:
Erysipelas is a Streptococcus pyogenes infection of the deep dermis and subcutis.
Treatment relies upon IV antibiotics such as benzylpenicillin and erythromycin. In a penicillin allergic patient a macrolide is the drugof choice from the above list.

stem:
A 60-year-old man presents with this lesion on his right arm which has been progressively enlarging since he ﬁrst noticed it two months ago.
What is your best diagnosis?
explanation:
Keratoacanthomas are now considered as a well-differentiated variant of squamous cell carcinoma. It presents as a rapidly enlargingnodule with a central keratinous crateriform scab. There are reports of spontaneous regression but generally they should be treatedwith full excision.
Acral lentiginous melanoma presents as a dark brown to black plaque or nodule on acral sites.
Actinic keratosis presents as a scaly, erythematous macule or papule on sun-damaged skin.
Basal cell carcinoma most commonly presents as an ulcerated nodule with pearly, rolled edges with telangiectasias.
Viral warts present as verrucous papules, usually of a ﬁliform nature.

stem:
A 25-year-old man presents with a single, painless, indurated ulcer on his penile shaft for the past one week. Several small, painless, inguinallymph nodes were palpable bilaterally. His last unprotected sexual encounter was with a prostitute three weeks prior to presentation.
Which of the following laboratory investigations will help to conﬁrm the diagnosis?
options: Culture of secretions from the ulcer on Thayer-Martin medium
Fungal culture from a scraping of the ulcer edge
KOH preparation of secretions from the ulcer
Darkﬁeld microscopy of secretions from the ulcer
Bacterial culture of secretions from the ulcer
explanation:
This patient presents with a chancre of primary syphilis. It usually occurs two to six weeks after exposure. It is caused by thespirochaete Treponema pallidum. Diagnosis of primary syphilis may be conﬁrmed either with darkﬁeld microscopy of secretionsfrom the ulcer or with serology.
Bacterial culture of secretions from the ulcer is

stem:
A 13-year-old girl presents with this nail abnormality which is seen on almost all of her ﬁnger and toe nails bilaterally. Her mother says thatshe ﬁrst noticed it about two months ago.
What further history or examination ﬁnding would aid in your diagnosis?
options: Family member that was recently treated for tinea pedis
A localised scaly patch of alopecia on her scalp
Episode of severe dengue fever two months prior to presentation
Treatment with minocycline for moderately severe acne
explanation:
This patient has Beau's lines, a benign nail condition that presents as a jagged transverse groove on the nail plate corresponding toan episode of nail growth arrest, which can occur during an episode of severe medical illness. It usually affects several nails.
The clinical description of localised scaly patch of alopecia on her scalp is consistent with tinea capitis. Fungal nail infections presentwith thickening and discolouration of the nail plate with prominent subungual debris. It usually only affects one or several nails.
Nail psoriasis presents with pitting, onycholysis, subungual debris and yellowish nail discolouration.
Fungal nail infections present with thickening and discolouration of the nail plate with prominent subungual debris. It usually onlyaffects one or several nails.
Minocycline treatment can lead to discolouration of nails.

stem:
A 44-year-old HIV seropositive man presented to the clinic with this rash.
What agent should be used to treat this condition?
explanation: The rash shown is typical of herpes zoster, which should be treated with aciclovir.

stem:
A 47-year-old lady presented two weeks after returning from a holiday in the Caribbean complaining of an intensely pruritic rash on herabdomen.
What is the causative organism?
explanation: The ﬁgure shows cutaneous larva migrans (creeping eruption).

stem:
A 16-year-old boy presents with these asymptomatic, skin-coloured lesions on his face for the past three months.
Which of the following treatments is an option for treating this patient?
explanation:
This patient has molluscum contagiosum, presenting as multiple skin-coloured, dome-shaped, umbilicated papules. It is mostcommon in children.
Treatment options for molluscum include watchful waiting (especially in children), cryotherapy, topical imiquimod and topicalcantharidin. Oral cimetidine may also be attempted in some patients especially those with widespread lesions.
Oral aciclovir and topical ketoconazole are not indicated for patients with molluscum.

stem:
A 15-year-old girl presents with a one year history of a photo-distributed rash occurring on her face and dorsal arms. She describes the rashas small red bumps, that would appear a few hours after sun-exposure and would resolve after a few days without scarring.
She is otherwise well with no other complaints, and laboratory tests were normal.
What is your best diagnosis?
explanation:
Polymorphous light eruption presents most commonly in young females. Various morphologies have been described, for example,macules, papules, patches or plaques. However, in a given patient, the rash usually appears the same whenever it recurs. Itcommonly occurs a few hours after sun-exposure and resolves after a few days, without scarring.
Acute lupus erythematosus may present with a similar rash to polymorphous light eruption. However, patients will usually haveother symptoms like joint pains, oral ulcers, hair loss, etc. They frequently have positive anti-nuclear antibodies.
Discoid lupus erythematosus presents with chronic scaly, erythematous-to-hyperpigmented papules and plaques that leave residualscars and dyspigmentation. The rash is worsened by sun-exposure.
Solar urticaria presents with urticaria upon sun-exposure. This usually resolves in a few hours instead of a few days.
Patients with xeroderma pigmentosum present with exquisite sun sensitivity from a very young age. They also present with multiplesolar lentigines, nevi and malignant skin tumours, for example, basal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma and malignantmelanoma.

stem:
A 65-year-old woman presents with extensive blisters and erosions on her trunk and limbs for the past one month.
She denies any new medications in the last one year. On further examination, there is no mucosal involvement.
What is your ﬁrst line of treatment?
explanation:
This patient presents with bullous pemphigoid. She has multiple tense blisters that rupture with residual erosions. In view of theextensive involvement, oral corticosteroids are indicated as ﬁrst line therapy.
Oral ketoconazole is wrong as there is no evidence of fungal disease in this patient.
Oral methotrexate may be added if there is poor response to oral corticosteroids or as a steroid sparing agent. Other steroid sparingagents include dapsone, azathioprine and mycophenolate mofetil.
Topical coal tar is not indicated in the treatment of bullous pemphigoid. It is used mainly in patients with psoriasis.

stem:
This 20-year-old woman presents with this asymptomatic pigmentary condition on bilateral arms and legs.
Which of the following conditions has been reported as an association?
explanation:
This patient has vitiligo. The condition presents with these typical well demarcated depigmented patches.
It is associated with a higher incidence of other autoimmune conditions in patients and their relatives, for example:Autoimmune thyroiditisPernicious anaemiaAlopecia areata, andDiabetes mellitus.
The incidences of the other conditions listed here have not been reported to be increased in patients with vitiligo.

stem:
A 56-year-old seaman presents to his general practitioner with this appearance on the front of his legs.
He has had this lesion for at least one year and has received treatment with topical steroids and courses of antibiotics. Despite this the lesionhas deteriorated. The lesion is painless and recently he has noticed that the centre has broken down and is slightly oozing.
He has a ﬁve year history of diabetes mellitus and receives metformin 500 mg tds. He has also undergone dermatological surgery for skinmalignancies on his face over the last six years.
What is this skin lesion?
explanation:
Necrobiosis lipoidica is a disorder of collagen degeneration with a granulomatous response, thickening of blood vessel walls, and fatdeposition.
The exact cause of necrobiosis lipoidica is unknown, but the leading theory of necrobiosis lipoidica has focused on diabeticmicroangiopathy.
Necrobiosis is often mistaken for eczema but rather than responding to steroids may actually deteriorate. Occasionally ulceration ofthe lesion may occur.
Necrobiosis is typically painless.

stem: What is the diagnosis?

This patient has hypertension and is an insulin dependent diabetic. She developed this painless lesion over several weeks.
What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Necrobiosis lipoidica is a disorder of collagen degeneration with a granulomatous response, thickening of blood vessel walls, and fatdeposition.
The exact cause of necrobiosis lipoidica is unknown, but the leading theory of necrobiosis lipoidica has focused on diabeticmicroangiopathy.

stem:
A 31-year-old man was referred to the dermatology clinic after developing a scaly rash on his arms and legs, predominantly on the knees andelbows. The rash had been present for four weeks.
He had a history of hypertension and had been started on treatment with furosemide and rampiril by his general practitioner six monthspreviously. He also had a long history of bipolar disorder and had been started on lithium three months previously by his psychiatrist havingbeen taking chlorpromazine for ﬁve years. Six weeks previously he had been given a course of oxytetracycline for acne.
Which of his medications is most likely to have precipitated the rash?
explanation:
The clinical history gives a good description of psoriasis. Lithium is the most likely precipitant.
Several drugs are known to exacerbate or trigger the onset of psoriasis, including:Beta blockersLithiumAntimalarials, andNon-steroidal anti-inﬂammatory drugs (NSAIDs).
Reactions may occur from less than one month to one year after the medication is initiated.
Treatment of drug-induced psoriasis comprises withdrawal of all beta-blocking medications, NSAIDs, antimalarials and lithium,unless absolutely necessary.
Skin punch biopsy may be performed to exclude other forms of erythroderma or pustulosis.
Bed rest, bland topical compresses, and low potency topical steroids are useful. Frequent emollient use is advisable.
Etretinate, methotrexate, or phototherapy might be considered.
Chlorpromazine may be associated with the development of drug-induced lupus.

stem:
A 65-year-old woman presents with extensive blisters and erosions on her trunk and limbs for the past one month.
She denies any new medications in the last one year. There is no mucosal involvement.
What will a skin biopsy most likely reveal?
options: Inﬂammatory cells within the septa of the subcutaneous fat (panniculitis)
Subcorneal blister ﬁlled with numerous neutrophils
Thickening of the stratum corneum (hyperkeratosis) and spongiosis within the epidermis
explanation:
This patient presents with bullous pemphigoid. She has multiple tense blisters that rupture with residual erosions. Skin biopsy willreveal a subepidermal blister with an inﬁltrate of eosinophils. Direct immunoﬂuorescence studies will reveal IgG and C3 in thebasement membrane zone.
Inﬂammatory cells within the septa of the subcutaneous fat (panniculitis describes septal panniculitis, where there is aninﬂammatory inﬁltrate within the septa of the subcutaneous fat. The commonest cause is erythema nodosum.
Intraepidermal blister with acantholytic cells is seen in the pemphigus group of disease (pemphigus vulgaris and pemphigusfoliaceus). Clinically, they present with ﬂaccid blisters as the split in the skin is more superﬁcial.
Subcorneal blister ﬁlled with numerous neutrophils describes a superﬁcial pustule which may be seen in pustular drug eruptions andpustular psoriasis.

stem:
A 30-year-old man is seen with recurrent episodes of guttate psoriasis. He has been prone to recurrent episodes of tonsillitis and these havetriggered several episodes of the psoriasis.
He has come to see you again with a post-tonsillitis guttate psoriasis eruption across his trunk and limbs. It is affecting less than 10% of hisbody surface area.
In terms of the management and prevention of guttate psoriasis in this gentleman, which of the following options should be considered?
options: Referral to an ear, nose, and throat specialist
Prescribe a ten day course oral penicillin 500 mg QDS
Prescribe a seven day course of oral erythromycin 500 mg QDS
Prescribe prophylactic oral erythromycin 500 mg BD long term
Prescribe prophylactic oral penicillin 500 mg BD long term
explanation:
There is no clear study evidence to support the use of antibiotics or tonsillectomy in managing or preventing guttate psoriasis afterstreptococcal throat infections. However, there are recommendations based on expert opinion (from NICE and the BritishAssociation of Dermatologists) that tonsillectomy may be an option in those suffering with recurrent guttate psoriasis triggered byepisodes of tonsillitis. In such cases referral to ENT should be considered and discussed with the patient.
Further reading:
NICE Guidelines: Psoriasis

stem:
This patient presented with a three month history of a gradually enlarging rash on her foot.
She had a past history of rheumatoid arthritis. Urine dipstick was negative and a fasting blood glucose was normal.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Necrobiosis lipoidica is a disorder of collagen degeneration with a granulomatous response, thickening of blood vessel walls, and fatdeposition.
It is usually related to diabetes, but can also occur in patients with rheumatoid arthritis, as in this patient. Necrobiosis may precedesymptoms and signs of diabetes by several months. The exact cause of necrobiosis lipoidica is unknown, but the leading theory ofnecrobiosis lipoidica in diabetes has focused on diabetic microangiopathy.
Necrobiosis is often mistaken for eczema, but rather than responding to steroids it may actually deteriorate.
Occasionally ulceration of the lesion may occur.

stem:
This 35-year-old lady was referred to the outpatient clinic for advice regarding persistent acne.
She has been married for several years but does not have any children. She is a smoker and works as a secretary.
All the basic observations were within normal limits, however glycosuria was noted on urine dipstick testing.
From the given history, what is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The slide shows axillary acanthosis nigricans.

stem:
A 22-year-old female student presents with generalised pruritus of six weeks duration.
She has little other history of note and has otherwise been well. This itching has deteriorated over this time and is particularly worse at night.She has been unaware of any rashes and denies taking any prescribed drugs. There is no history of atopy.
She shares a ﬂat with her boyfriend and drinks approximately 12 units per week and smokes cannabis occasionally.
On examination, there is little of note except there are some scratch marks over the shoulders and back and she has some erythemabetween the ﬁngers. Otherwise cardiovascular, respiratory and abdominal examination is normal.
Which of the following therapies would be most appropriate treatment for this patient?
explanation:
This patient has scabies, a highly contagious disease caused by the mite Sarcoptes scabiei, and is quite common in the sexuallyactive.
It is well recognised to cause generalised pruritus and one should make a careful examination between the ﬁnger spaces forburrows.
Appropriate treatment includes permethrin cream, topical benzyl benzoate, and malathion. The permethrin cream doesn't have anydirect effect on the pruritis itself but helps to settle symptoms indirectly by killing the mite, which is the root cause. You shouldcounsel your patients that it may take longer for the itching to settle as the allergic reaction to the mite abates and that the creamshould be appplied everywhere below the neck, not merely where there is rash present.
References:
British National Formulary: Permethrin
BMJ Best Practice: Scabies
Primary Care Dermatology Society: Scabies

stem:
A 24-year-old man presents with a widespread, acute skin eruption consisting of red, slightly scaly 'drop-like' skin lesions on his trunk andlimbs. This eruption followed a throat infection which has now settled.
The skin lesions are diffuse and cover about 25% of his body. He works as a lifeguard at the local swimming pool and so he is concernedabout the appearance of the rash.
He is usually ﬁt and well with no signiﬁcant past medical history or drug allergies.
Which of the following is the most appropriate management approach?
options: Prescribe a seven day course of oral prednisolone 30 mg daily
Prescribe a ten day course of oral penicillin 500 mg QDS
explanation:
This patient has guttate psoriasis. Guttate psoriasis is typically an acute eruption of drop-like psoriatic skin lesions. The trunk andlimbs are usually affected and onset can occur after a streptococcal throat infection.
No treatment is a viable option in many patients with guttate psoriasis, as it is usually self-limiting and typically will resolve withinthree - four months. No treatment would be appropriate if lesions are not widespread (<10% body surface area) and the person isnot impacted physically, psychologicall,y or socially by the problem. 
If the lesions are not widespread (<10% body surface area) and treatment is desired, then topical treatment can be used as would beused for any trunk or limb psoriasis.
If lesions are widespread (>10% body surface area), as is the case in this scenario, then it is appropriate to refer them urgently to adermatologist as phototherapy can be considered.
Although guttate psoriasis can be triggered by an acute sore throat, it is not recommended to treat guttate psoriasis with anti-streptococcal antibiotics.
Further reading:
NICE Guidelines: Psoriasis

stem:
This 71-year-old lady presented with several months history of facial discomfort and a perceived change in her facial expression.
She also complained of having 'gritty' eyes.
What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
The photograph shows typical features of systemic sclerosis, including facial telangiectasia, small mouth, beaking of the nose.
Systemic sclerosis is a small vessel vasculitis that causes deposition of connective tissue in oragns. The classical feature of thecondition is deposition in the skin, known as scleroderma, which is why the condition is often known just as 'scleroderma'.

stem:
A 46-year-old man presents with an extensive pruritic rash shown in picture A.
Two weeks previously he had a sore throat with the appearance shown in picture B.
What is the cause of the rash?
explanation:
Guttate psoriasis takes its name from the appearance of the lesions which are 'drop like'. It is a common presentation of psoriasis inchildren and young adults and may often follow an upper respiratory tract infection especially streptococcal.
Pityriasis rosea is of unknown aetiology and is a widespread pink patchy rash that appears after a 'herald patch'.
Pityriasis rubra pilaris is a papulosquamous disorder of unknown aetiology which presents as red-orange plaques. It is a cause oferythroderma.

stem:
This 45-year-old man presents with these lesions on his face for the past three years.
The lesions are worse after sun-exposure. He has no systemic complaints.
Which of the following treatment options is indicated in this patient?
explanation:
This patient has discoid lupus erythematosus.
He presents with scaly, hyperpigmented, erythematous plaques on sun-exposed areas. This condition may lead to severe scarring.
Treatment options include:Topical potent corticosteroidsTopical calcineurin inhibitorsIntralesional corticosteroidsAnti-malarials, andOral corticosteroids.

stem:
A 28-year-old woman is seen with a rash. This started within a few days of an acute sore throat. The throat has improved but two weeks laterthe rash persists.
On examination, there are multiple, small, red, scaly plaques that affect the trunk. The lesions cover only about 5% of her body surface area.She is completely well in herself and the rash is not bothering her in terms of appearance or any symptoms.
Which is the most appropriate management approach?
explanation:
This patient has guttate psoriasis. Guttate psoriasis is typically an acute eruption of drop-like psoriatic skin lesions. The trunk andlimbs are usually affected and onset can occur after a streptococcal throat infection.
No treatment is a viable option as it is usually self-limiting and typically will resolve within three - four months. This is particularly thecase if lesions are not widespread (<10% body surface area) and the person is not impacted physically, psychologically, or socially bythe problem. If the lesions are not widespread (<10% body surface area) and treatment is desired, then topical treatment can beused as would be used for any trunk or limb psoriasis.
If lesions are widespread (>10% body surface area) then it is appropriate to refer them urgently to a dermatologist as phototherapycan be considered.
Further reading:
NICE Guidelines: Psoriasis

stem:
A 42-year-old lady with known psoriasis presents to you with symptoms of a severe ﬂare-up. The patient is very upset and confesses that herdisease is affecting her quality of life.
She is presently on methotrexate and folic acid as long term maintenance, after a failed trial of phototherapy and an apparent allergy tocyclosporin.
Which of the following would you consider as the next step in her management?
explanation:
Psoriasis can have a signiﬁcant psychosocial effect on the patient. Control of the disease is incredibly important to maintain a normallife for psoriasis sufferers.
Biological immune modifying agents licensed to treat moderate to severe psoriasis, include TNF alpha-blockers (e.g. etanercept,inﬂiximab, adalimumab) and blockers of interleukin 12/23 (i.e. Ustekinumab).
Treatment for psoriasis can be grouped into topical or systemic. Mild to moderate disease can be controlled via topical treatmentssuch as:coal tartopical steroidstopical tacrolimus, andphototherapy.
Systemic treatments include:methotrexatecyclosporin, andbiological immune modifying agents (as listed above).

stem: What is the commonest cause for this appearance?
explanation:
The slide shows typical target lesions of erythema multiforme (EM).
Herpes simplex virus infection is the commonest cause. Other common causes include infection with Mycoplasma andStreptococci.
EM may also:Be idiopathicBe drug-induced (sulfonamides, sulphonylureas, barbiturates)Occur in systemic diseases (SLE, inﬂammatory bowel disease, malignancy).

stem:
This 72-year-old lady presented with dysphagia.
Which of the following autoantibodies is highly speciﬁc for this condition?
explanation:
The slide shows the hands of a patient with systemic sclerosis/CREST (the distinction cannot be made on the basis of the picturealone).
Rheumatoid factor is non-speciﬁc and is positive in 25% of cases; ANF is positive 95%.
Autoantibodies strongly associated with SSc include antinucleolar antibodies and anti-U3 nucleolar RNP.
Anticentromere antibodies are strongly associated with CREST syndrome. Anti-SSA (Ro) and anti-SSB (La) antibodies are seen in SScassociated with Sjögren's syndrome.
Anticardiolipin antibodies may be found in association with SLE.
Antimitochondrial antibodies are associated with primary biliary cirrhosis.

stem:
A 50-year-old woman presents with this non-pruritic rash on her arms and legs for the past month.
She gives a history that she has been able to eat only soft foods for the past three months due to dental problems. She also complains of atraumatic wound on her hand that has taken a longer time to heal.
What is your best diagnosis?
explanation:
Scurvy is a result of vitamin C deﬁciency. It is required for collagen synthesis. The ﬁnding shown is peri-follicuar haemorrhage. Otherﬁndings include bleeding gums, corkscrew hair and poor wound healing. High-dose vitamin C replacement will usually lead to rapidresolution of symptoms in a few days.
Beri-beri is a result of deﬁciency of thiamine (vitamin B1). It can present with neurological, cardiovascular and gastrointestinalsymptoms.
Pellagra is a result of niacin deﬁciency. It can present with clinical symptoms and signs starting with the four Ds:dermatitis (photodistributed)dementiadiarrhoea, and

stem:
This 40-year-old female is admitted with a two month history of abdominal pains, watery diarrhoea and has noted this extensive rash.
What is this rash?
explanation:
The symptoms with this rash, which is typical of necrolytic migratory erythema, suggest a glucagonoma.
Other features of glucagonoma include:Diabetes mellitusHypoaminoacidaemiaCheilosisNormochromic normocytic anaemiaVenous thrombosisNeuropsychiatric features.

stem:
A 40-year-old man presents with this chronic rash on his right middle ﬁnger for the past six months.
He is otherwise healthy and his hobbies include tennis, golf and rearing ornamental ﬁsh.
By which organism is this most likely to be caused?
explanation:
This patient has a ﬁsh-tank granuloma, caused by the atypical mycobacterium, Mycobacterium marinum. It is found in ornamentalﬁsh and is commonly seen in individuals who rear ﬁsh as a hobby.
Candida albicans causes cutaneous candidiasis which usually affects intertriginous areas with typical satellite lesions.
Mycobacterium marinum is the causative organism so it would be wrong to suggest that no organism is usually found in thisinstance.
Sporothrix schenckii is a fungus that causes sporotrichosis which presents with erythematous papules and nodules along alymphatic.

stem:
This 60-year-old man presented to his general practitioner with a three month history of proximal muscle weakness. There is a barelyperceptible purple rash on sun exposed areas, but more noticeable over the knuckles.
He was a smoker of 20 cigarettes a day for 40 years.
What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Dermatomyositis is an autoimmune disease characterised by polymyositis and a skin rash.
The classic purple (heliotrope) rash is seen on sun-exposed areas, especially the eyelids, nose, cheeks, forehead, knees, knuckles andaround the nail beds. The rash may be pruritic.

stem:
A 25-year-old man presents with this rash on both ankles for the past three years.
He admits to scratching these areas frequently, especially during times of stress.
What is your diagnosis?
explanation:
Lichen simplex chronicus (LSC) presents with hyperpigmented, scaly, licheniﬁed plaques. Patients may volunteer a history of chronicscratching or manipulation, especially during times of stress. The ankles are common sites for LSC.
Psoriasis vulgaris presents with well-demarcated, scaly, pinkish plaques.
Squamous cell carcinomas occur in older patients and present with an eroded or ulcerated, hyperkeratotic plaque, nodule ortumour. They rarely present with symmetric bilateral involvement.
Subacute lupus erythematosus does not commonly occur on the lower limbs, unless there is widespread involvement of the head,trunk and upper extremities. It presents either with psoriasiform or annular plaques.
Tinea, although common on the legs, presents with scaly, annular plaques with central clearing.

stem:
This 45-year-old white female presented to her general practitioner asking for advice regarding removal of these lesions for cosmeticreasons.
What additional investigation should be performed?
explanation:
This is a case of molluscum contagiosum.
Such umbilicated, pearly papules 2-5 mm in diameter are seen in patients with advanced HIV/AIDS (CD4 count less than 200cells/mm).
They are caused by a DNA pox virus called molluscum contagiosum virus (MCV).
They commonly occur on the face, especially near the eyelids; they also occur on genitals and trunk.
They should be treated with cryotherapy, liquid nitrogen or curettage.

stem:
An 18-year-old female who has had stable atopic dermatitis presents with this worsening rash over the right side of her face and neck overthe past one week.
She has been only on daily moisturisers and topical corticosteroid therapy prior to this ﬂare. She denies any new contactants. She was alsonoted to have a low-grade temperature of 38.1°C.
What treatment should be rendered?
explanation:
This patient presents with eczema herpeticum.
It is a cutaneous infection caused by herpes virus, seen in patients with pre-existing inﬂammatory skin disorders, for example,eczema, Darier's disease.
Patients present with new onset of clustered blisters and erosions over an erythematous base. The eruption can be widespread andpatients may be ill. Lesions may be secondarily impetiginised with Staphylococcus infection.
Treatment requires systemic anti-virals, for example, aciclovir. Systemic antibiotics may be required if lesions are secondarilyimpetiginised.
The patient does not present with a fungal infection and will not require treatment of topical or oral anti-fungals.

stem:
A 75-year-old man presents with this lesion on his scalp for the past three months which has been slowly increasing in size. It occasionallybleeds after minor trauma. He has been on aspirin for previous strokes.
What is your best diagnosis?
explanation:
Angiosarcomas are malignant vascular tumours most commonly seen in elderly men. They most commonly occur on the scalp andforehead. They present an inﬁltrative vascular patch or plaque with super-imposed nodules which may bleed with minor trauma.They have a poor prognosis. Angiosarcomas can also occur in areas of chronic lymphoedema.
Bruises occur after trauma and usually resolve over a few weeks in stages, ﬁrst becoming purpuric, then dark grey or green.
Kaposi's sarcoma is most commonly seen in patients with HIV. It can also occur in elderly men without HIV. It most commonlypresents on the lower limbs and patients may present with multiple lesions. It is considered a low-grade vascular malignancy and isassociated with HHV-8 infection.

stem: What is the diagnosis in this 78-year-old man?
explanation:
Pemphigoid is a disease of the elderly (over 60 years) characterised by the development of large blisters that heal without scarring.
The condition is caused by immunoglobulin (IgG) autoantibodies against components of the basement membrane.

stem:
A 48- year-old man with diabetes mellitus presents with a 24 hour history of an increasingly painful left leg.
What is the most likely causative organism?
explanation:
Ascending cellulitis is shown.
Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococci are the commonest causative organisms.
Group B Streptococcus has a predilection for diabetic patients and is the likeliest causative organism in this scenario.

stem:
A 70-year-old man presents with a growth on his nose for the past six months. He is a retired sailor.
What is your best diagnosis?
explanation:
This patient presents with a typical 'rodent ulcer' with rolled pearly edges and small telangiectasias. It is the commonest malignantskin tumour and most commonly occurs in elderly patients with sun-damaged skin.
Actinic keratosis is a pre-malignant condition, seen most commonly on sun-damaged skin in older patients. It presents as a small,scaly, erythematous macule or papule. Less than 10% of actinic keratoses progress to invasive squamous cell carcinoma.
Angiosarcoma is a malignant vascular tumour seen most commonly in elderly males. It most commonly affects the scalp andforehead and presents with a purpuric patch or plaque, often with nodules that may bleed.
Keratoacanthoma can be considered a well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma, most commonly occurring in elderly patients. Itpresents as a crateriform nodule with central scabbing.

stem:
This gentleman ﬁrst presented in his early 20s with haemoptysis. He has required intermittent blood transfusions throughout his life.
What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Typical telangiectasia of hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia are seen.
The condition is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait; sporadic cases also occur.
Patients typically present early in adult life with anaemia due to occult bleeding from gastrointestinal telangiectasiae.
Lesions commonly occur in the mouth and on the face.

stem:
A 20-year-old male presents with this rash on his scalp for the past six months. It is only mildly itchy.
His father has had a similar rash since he was a teenager.
What is your ﬁrst line of treatment?
explanation:
This patient presents with typical scalp and hairline psoriasis. First line treatment would involve topical corticosteroid preparations aswell as medicated shampoos containing zinc, coal tar, salicylic acid, corticosteroids or ciclopirox.
Miconazole is an imidazole antifungal topical preparation and is indicated for superﬁcial cutaneous fungal infections.
Oral griseofulvin is indicated for tinea capitis which presents with alopecia and localised scaly patches on the scalp, associated withshort, broken hair shafts.
Oral methotrexate is indicated for moderate and severe psoriasis not responding to topical therapies.
Topical permethrin is used to treat scabies infestations. Scabies does not affect the scalp in older children and adults.

stem:
An 82-year-old Jewish lady presented with the following rash:
Immunoﬂuorescent staining of a skin biopsy from this patient showed intercellular deposition of IgG within the epidermis.
What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
The slide shows the characteristic rash of pemphigus vulgaris. Blisters are thin-walled and rupture easily (intact blisters are rarelyseen). Large surface areas of the body can be affected and the mortality without treatment is high.
Mucosal involvement is common at presentation (unlike pemphigoid). Treatment is with high-dose corticosteroids.
Pemphigus vulgaris is a blistering disease seen predominantly in patients ages 50-60, but can affect many ages. It is characterised bythe formation of thin-walled blisters that rupture easily. Immunoﬂuorescent staining of a biopsy sample shows deposition ofimmunoglobulin (IgG) directed against to keratinocyte desmosomes and to desmosome-free areas of the keratinocyte cellmembrane, resulting in a 'chicken wire' appearance. The binding of autoantibodies results in a loss of cell-to-cell adhesion, a processtermed acantholysis.

stem:
A 50-year-old wine grower presented with a six month history of recurrent blisters on the dorsum of his hand. These tended to be worse inthe summer and were occasionally itchy.
He had previously lived in the tropics when he was in the army. His only medication was bendroﬂumethiazide for hypertension and he hadbeen on the same treatment for the previous three years.
A picture of the hands is shown.
What is the diagnosis?
explanation: Out of the possible answers porphyria cutanea tarda is the most likely to induce a blistering rash on the dorsum of the hand.

stem:
This 30-year-old man developed this mildly pruritic rash on his lower abdomen, which started about a week ago. He gives a history ofspending some time on the beaches of Brazil a week before the rash began.
What treatment should you prescribe?
explanation:
From the history of spending time on a tropical beach and the clinical picture of a creeping eruption, this patient has cutaneous larvamigrans. It is caused by hookworms, most commonly Ancylostoma brasiliense and A. caninum.
The disease is self-limiting but the duration of disease varies considerably. Oral ivermectin in a single dose of 200 µg/kg body weightis the main treatment. Other treatment options include oral albendazole or topical thiabendazole.
Oral aciclovir is used to treat herpetic infections or infections caused by varicella-zoster virus.
Terbinaﬁne is an anti-fungal used to treat dermatophyte infections.
Miconazole is a topical anti-fungal.

stem:
A 40-year-old man presents with a three day history of a generalised painful rash associated with erosions in his mouth and genitals. He wasrecently started on allopurinol for gout. He is febrile and appears ill.
On examination, there are dusky, targetoid papules and plaques on his face, trunk and limbs, which desquamate easily on rubbing the skin.
What is your best diagnosis?
options: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS)
explanation:
This patient has toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN), a severe idiosyncratic drug reaction, with a high morbidity and mortality rate.Commonly implicated drugs include anti-epileptics, penicillins, NSAIDS and allopurinol. Patients present with erythematous-to-dusky plaques and targetoid lesions that progress rapidly to painful, full-thickness, epidermal desquamation involving more than30% of body surface area. Mucosal involvement is also seen. Nikolsky's sign is elicited when rubbing of the skin results indesquamation.
DRESS is another severe drug eruption characterised by generalised erythematous rash often associated with facial oedema,involvement of internal organs (liver dysfunction), haematologic abnormalities (eosinophilia) and systemic illness (fever).
Erythema multiforme presents with target lesions on the acral areas most commonly associated with herpes infections.
Fixed drug eruption presents with one or several erythematous-to-dusky patches or plaques with central blister. It is not associatedwith systemic symptoms and patients are not ill.
Pemphigus vulgaris presents with ﬂaccid blisters and erosions as well as mucosal involvement. The history is not as acute as in TENand drugs are less often implicated. Nikolsky's sign is also positive in pemphigus.

stem:
This 55-year-old patient presented with a four month history of nausea and weight loss (8 kg).
He complained of vague abdominal discomfort with no clear exacerbating or relieving factors. His only past history was of a partialgastrectomy twenty years previously for a gastric ulcer. He was not taking any prescribed medications.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Acanthosis nigricans (pictured) has a characteristic hyperpigmented, velvety surface. It frequently occurs in the axillae, groins and inthe skin fold of the neck and occasionally on the dorsum of the hand.

stem:
On skin examination of a patient, you notice multiple, small, raised, slightly dome-shaped lesions containing purulent material.
How are these lesions best described?
explanation:
Pustules are small elevations of the skin containing cloudy or purulent material, usually consisting of necrotic inﬂammatory cells.
Bullae are large vesicles containing serous ﬂuid.
Fissures are cracks in the skin that are narrow but deep.
Telangiectasias are collections of enlarged capillaries visible on the skin or mucous membranes.
Ulcers are seen as discontinuity of the skin with complete loss of the epidermis and often portions of the dermis and subcutaneousfat.

stem:
A 47-year-old Turkish man presented to the Emergency department with this lesion on his arm.
He also complained of discomfort in the left axilla.
The lesion had developed over a period of two weeks and was painless. There was no past history of note. He had recently returned from avacation to his parents' goat farm in Turkey.
What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
The slide shows the typical appearance of cutaneous anthrax, caused by Bacillus anthracis.
Cutaneous disease is the commonest form of the infection in humans and is usually due to contact with infected animals or animalproducts. Anthrax is endemic to herd animals in some parts of the world.

stem:
This 72-year-old lady presented with a two day history of fever and painful facial rash.
What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Erysipelas is a Streptococcus pyogenes infection of the deep dermis and subcutis.
Treatment relies upon IV antibiotics such as benzylpenicillin and erythromycin.
Complications include sepsis, cerebral abscess and venous sinus thrombosis.
